content.text:
**Robot failure forensics is a credible direction. Your biggest gap is proving that Trace helps an engineer finish an investigation faster—and proving which part of that improvement comes from OpenTSLM.** Adding an agent and RAG can support that outcome, but doesn’t establish it by itself.

I checked the latest `origin/main`, the implementation, and the original challenge brief. The brief explicitly rewards useful problems, rigorous evaluation, and clear demonstrations. Its agentic bonus concerns **dataset sourcing and preparation**; a conversational agent is not a requirement. :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/sametdegirmenci/Downloads/Aionic_Temporal_AI_Hackathon.pdf" purpose="source"}

I would prioritize these six things.

**1. Make one investigation outcome the product promise.**

Use this positioning:

> **Trace helps robotics engineers turn a recorded contact incident into an evidence-backed investigation report: when it happened, which signals changed, how similar incidents compare, and what needs further inspection.**

That gives your proposed features a purpose. The deliverable is a report an engineer can use or hand to a teammate.

For the challenge, narrow the demonstrated claim to **contact-event triage**. Your dataset contains controlled collision/contact experiments; it does not establish actual failed production runs, safety-stop causes, or repairs. Its documented hammer-versus-gloved-hand confound also limits what “intentional versus accidental” classification proves. See the [dataset card](/Users/sametdegirmenci/Downloads/ysamet/model_training/docs/dataset.md).

There is an established market for this workflow. Foxglove already offers [agents for robotics data](https://www.foxglove.dev/blog/foxglove-goes-agentic) and [comparisons across recordings](https://foxglove.dev/blog/compare-robot-recordings-across-runs). My inference: **“chat with robot logs” is too broad to differentiate Trace. Evaluated interpretation of torque events, with inspectable evidence, is a sharper contribution.**

**2. Finish the comparison that answers “Why OpenTSLM?”**

This is the highest-priority engineering task. A transparent feature baseline already exists in [baseline.py](/Users/sametdegirmenci/Downloads/ysamet/model_training/src/robot_observability/baseline.py); I did not find a checked-in comparison report.

Use three systems:

| System | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Signal features + logistic regression | Can inexpensive conventional methods solve the task? |
| Llama with a documented numerical/text representation | Can an ordinary language model solve it? |
| Your trained OpenTSLM | What does the trained temporal model add? |

**Llama is a useful baseline, but should supplement the signal baseline.** Specify its exact model, input representation, and training regime. A fine-tuned OpenTSLM versus zero-shot Llama comparison is valid when labeled clearly; it does not isolate architecture from training.

One concrete issue: the current signal baseline evaluates the full test split, while the OpenTSLM evaluator defaults to a 512-example subset. Compare **identical example IDs**, with identical targets.

Report semantics macro-F1, contact F1, onset error **with coverage**, output validity, latency, and test recording/window counts. Treat joint scores as agreement with derived signal labels, not physical impact localization.

If the simple baseline wins some tasks, use it for those tasks. An honest hybrid system is a stronger submission than an inflated model claim.

**3. Measure the business benefit with a small user study.**

Ask three to five robotics engineers to complete several matched investigations:

- Find the relevant interval.
- Describe the event and identify the strongest signal changes.
- Produce a short report with supporting evidence.

Compare manual chart inspection with Trace; counterbalance task order and use different matched cases to reduce learning effects. Measure completion time, correctness, and unsupported conclusions.

The slide you want is:

> “Across N participants and M investigations, median time to a correct report changed from X to Y.”

Those values must be measured. Even a small, clearly labeled formative study makes the business argument more concrete. Reduced repeat failures and downtime remain future outcomes until you measure them.

**4. Build one complete investigation path across several real recordings.**

Your most valuable product extension is:

**Select incident → inspect measurements and prediction → compare a similar event → export the investigation.**

Start with a small curated set containing collision, intentional contact, and free motion. The current inference fixture only supplies raw 1 kHz torque within `[4, 9)` seconds of one recording; expanding raw-window access is a prerequisite for a credible cross-run demonstration.

For similarity, begin with normalized signal features and a visible distance measure. Show aligned traces so the engineer can judge whether the match is meaningful.

Export recording IDs, intervals, channels, measurements, model/checkpoint identity, source labels, and engineer notes. That creates the first useful building block for labeling and retraining cohorts.

**5. Give the agent a bounded investigation job; make RAG earn its place.**

Your proposed architecture makes sense when each component has a clear responsibility:

| Component | Useful responsibility |
|---|---|
| Measurements | Calculate peaks, changes, durations, and joint rankings |
| OpenTSLM | Predict event semantics from the telemetry |
| Incident retrieval | Find comparable recorded cases |
| Document RAG | Retrieve relevant procedures, manuals, or reviewed incident notes |
| Assistant | Assemble a cited report and identify missing evidence |

The compelling request is:

> “Investigate this event, compare it with similar recordings, and prepare a report showing the evidence and unresolved questions.”

Keep publisher annotations, measurements, predictions, and retrieved documents visibly distinct. Retrieve prior cases from an approved reference corpus; keep held-out answers out of evaluation retrieval.

**Web search should be optional background research.** It cannot establish why this specific robot stopped. For a repeatable demo, a small curated document collection is more useful than unrestricted searching.

I would keep the deterministic workflow initially. Add LLM tool selection only when you have several real investigation requests that require different tool sequences and can demonstrate an improvement.

**6. Make reliability and submission proof visible.**

The recorded 77.93% structured-output validity deserves attention: roughly one in five outputs failed that recorded criterion. The UI should preserve measured facts and clearly identify unavailable model conclusions.

Also verify the metric itself: the local parser’s validity measure accepts a JSON dictionary; that alone does not establish compliance with the full answer schema.

Finish with:

- A reproducible TimeNet build/load/validation receipt.
- One baseline comparison table tied to exact artifacts.
- One successful investigation and one honest failure or uncertain case.
- A two-minute demo ending with the exported report and measured benefit.

**My recommended next move is to freeze the shared evaluation examples and produce the three-system comparison, while the team recruits a few engineers for the timed investigation study.** Then extend raw recording access and build the report-and-comparison flow. Those steps directly strengthen technical credibility, business value, and the demo; broad RAG and web-search orchestration come afterward.

I made no repository changes during this strategy review.

+"""Dependency-free audit of frozen predictions; never fits or repairs a model.
+
+Missing/invalid predictions remain abstentions. Temporal MAE is conditional on a
+finite in-window estimate; success within tolerance uses all true contact events.
+"""
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+from collections import Counter
+import gzip
+import hashlib
+import json
+import math
+from pathlib import Path
+import random
+import statistics
+
+CLASSES = ("free", "intentional", "accidental")
+JOINTS = {f"J{i}" for i in range(1, 8)}
+KEYS = {"contact", "event_type", "onset_ms", "strongest_joint", "affected_joints",
+        "evidence_start_ms", "evidence_end_ms"}
+MODELS = {"features": "Signal features + logistic regression",
+          "opentslm": "OpenTSLM canary-v4 (trained Llama 3.2 1B)",
+          "qwen": "Qwen3-VL 4B, zero-shot plots",
+          "zero-signal": "OpenTSLM zero-signal ablation"}
+
+
+def read_bytes(path: Path) -> bytes:
+    data = path.read_bytes()
+    return gzip.decompress(data) if path.suffix == ".gz" else data
+
+
+def rows(path: Path) -> list[dict]:
+    return [json.loads(line) for line in read_bytes(path).splitlines() if line.strip()]
+
+
+def unique_index(items: list[dict]) -> dict[str, dict]:
+    result = {}
+    for row in items:
+        key = row["record_id"]
+        if key in result:
+            raise ValueError(f"Duplicate record ID: {key}")
+        result[key] = row
+    return result
+
+
+def time_valid(value: object, *, endpoint: bool = False) -> bool:
+    return (type(value) in (int, float) and math.isfinite(value)
+            and 0 <= value <= 1024 and (endpoint or value < 1024))
+
+
+def schema_valid(p: object) -> bool:
+    if not isinstance(p, dict) or set(p) != KEYS:
+        return False
+    if type(p["contact"]) is not bool or p["event_type"] not in CLASSES:
+        return False
+    affected = p["affected_joints"]
+    if (not isinstance(affected, list) or any(type(j) is not str or j not in JOINTS for j in affected)
+            or len(set(affected)) != len(affected)):
+        return False
+    if not p["contact"]:
+        return p["event_type"] == "free" and not affected and all(
+            p[k] is None for k in ("onset_ms", "strongest_joint", "evidence_start_ms", "evidence_end_ms"))
+    return (p["event_type"] != "free" and p["strongest_joint"] in affected
+            and time_valid(p["onset_ms"]) and time_valid(p["evidence_start_ms"])
+            and time_valid(p["evidence_end_ms"], endpoint=True)
+            and p["evidence_start_ms"] < p["evidence_end_ms"])
+
+
+def score(items: list[dict]) -> dict:
+    n = len(items)
+    if not n:
+        raise ValueError("Cannot score an empty evaluation")
+    confusion = {c: Counter() for c in CLASSES}
+    contact_confusion = {"false": Counter(), "true": Counter()}
+    valid = parsed = contact_valid = contact_correct = joint_correct = 0
+    errors = []
+    event_n = 0
+    affected_scores = []
+    for row in items:
+        target, p = row["target"], row.get("prediction")
+        parsed += isinstance(p, dict)
+        valid += schema_valid(p)
+        p = p if isinstance(p, dict) else {}
+        pred_class = p.get("event_type")
+        pred_class = pred_class if isinstance(pred_class, str) and pred_class in CLASSES else "abstain"
+        confusion[target["event_type"]][pred_class] += 1
+        contact = p.get("contact")
+        is_bool = type(contact) is bool
+        contact_valid += is_bool
+        contact_correct += is_bool and contact == target["contact"]
+        contact_confusion[str(target["contact"]).lower()][str(contact).lower() if is_bool else "abstain"] += 1
+        if target["contact"]:
+            event_n += 1
+            joint_correct += p.get("strongest_joint") == target["strongest_joint"]
+            onset = p.get("onset_ms")
+            if time_valid(onset):
+                errors.append(abs(onset - target["onset_ms"]))
+            affected = p.get("affected_joints")
+            if (isinstance(affected, list) and all(type(j) is str and j in JOINTS for j in affected)
+                    and len(set(affected)) == len(affected)):
+                truth, predicted = set(target["affected_joints"]), set(affected)
+                denominator = len(truth) + len(predicted)
+                affected_scores.append(2 * len(truth & predicted) / denominator if denominator else 1.0)
+            else:
+                affected_scores.append(0.0)
+    f1 = {}
+    for c in CLASSES:
+        tp = confusion[c][c]
+        fp = sum(confusion[other][c] for other in CLASSES if other != c)
+        fn = sum(confusion[c].values()) - tp
+        f1[c] = 2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn) if 2 * tp + fp + fn else 0.0
+    contact_f1 = {}
+    for c in ("false", "true"):
+        other = "true" if c == "false" else "false"
+        tp, fp = contact_confusion[c][c], contact_confusion[other][c]
+        fn = sum(contact_confusion[c].values()) - tp
+        contact_f1[c] = 2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn) if 2 * tp + fp + fn else 0.0
+    return {
+        "n": n, "contact_events": event_n,
+        "json_object_rate": parsed / n, "usable_summary_rate": valid / n,
+        "semantics_macro_f1": statistics.mean(f1.values()),
+        "semantics_accuracy": sum(confusion[c][c] for c in CLASSES) / n,
+        "semantics_per_class_f1": f1, "semantics_confusion": {c: dict(confusion[c]) for c in CLASSES},
+        "contact_answer_coverage": contact_valid / n, "contact_accuracy": contact_correct / n,
+        "contact_macro_f1": statistics.mean(contact_f1.values()),
+        "contact_positive_f1": contact_f1["true"],
+        "contact_confusion": {c: dict(contact_confusion[c]) for c in contact_confusion},
+        "strongest_joint_accuracy": joint_correct / event_n if event_n else None,
+        "affected_joint_set_f1_contact_only": statistics.mean(affected_scores) if affected_scores else None,
+        "onset_coverage": len(errors) / event_n if event_n else None,
+        "onset_mae_ms": statistics.mean(errors) if errors else None,
+        "onset_median_ae_ms": statistics.median(errors) if errors else None,
+        "onset_within_50ms_all_contacts": sum(e <= 50 for e in errors) / event_n if event_n else None,
+    }
+
+
+def validate_alignment(predictions: dict[str, list[dict]], records: list[dict], splits: dict) -> list[str]:
+    prepared = unique_index(records)
+    indices = {name: unique_index(items) for name, items in predictions.items()}
+    ids = sorted(next(iter(indices.values())))
+    if not ids:
+        raise ValueError("Empty evaluation")
+    for name, index in indices.items():
+        if set(index) != set(ids):
+            raise ValueError(f"Unequal test record IDs: {name}")
+        for key in ids:
+            if key not in prepared:
+                raise ValueError(f"Unknown prepared record: {key}")
+            record, row = prepared[key], index[key]
+            if record.get("split") != "test" or splits.get(record["session_id"]) != "test":
+                raise ValueError(f"Record is not in held-out test sessions: {key}")
+            if row.get("session_id", record["session_id"]) != record["session_id"]:
+                raise ValueError(f"Wrong session: {key}")
+            target = {k: record["onset_sample"] if k == "onset_ms" else record[k] for k in KEYS}
+            if row["target"] != target:
+                raise ValueError(f"Target mismatch for {name}: {key}")
+            row["session_id"] = record["session_id"]
+    return ids
+
+
+def bootstrap_difference(left: list[dict], right: list[dict], repeats: int, seed: int) -> dict:
+    """Paired recording-cluster bootstrap, OpenTSLM minus feature baseline."""
+    groups = {}
+    right_by_id = unique_index(right)
+    for row in left:

# Pilot: time to a correct investigation report

Status: protocol prepared; no participants recruited, no results collected. This document must not be presented as user-study evidence.

## Decision

Does Trace's evidence-linked analysis and export help robotics engineers complete a correct contact-event report faster than chart inspection? The buyer hypothesis is a robotics engineering or test lead responsible for incident review; the initial user is the engineer assembling the report.

## Protocol

Recruit 3–5 robotics engineers for a formative pilot. Ask first how they investigate a recorded incident, which artifacts they hand off, and what information is usually missing. Do not solicit a positive testimonial or prime them with a claimed time saving.

Prepare six matched cases across collision, intentional contact and free motion. Use development/validation recordings; do not tune the model with final test answers. Keep source labels hidden during tasks. Give both conditions the same telemetry and documentation. Match case difficulty by duration and signal strength; each participant sees distinct cases in each condition. Counterbalance case assignment and condition order.

Condition A: synchronized charts and ordinary numerical tools, without generated interpretations. Condition B: Trace with its actual measurements, model predictions, evidence links and export. Include at least one model failure or unavailable answer in B. Allow the same short tool familiarization in both conditions. Apply a five-minute task cap and retain incomplete attempts.

Each task asks the participant to locate the event, state its class or abstain, identify strongest signal changes, and produce a short evidence-backed report. A reviewer blinded to condition scores against publisher labels for class/onset and separately against deterministic measurements for joint quantities. Do not score a physical root-cause diagnosis: no such ground truth exists.

Record condition, order, case ID, elapsed seconds, completion, class correctness, onset error, measurement correctness, unsupported claims, tool failures and qualitative comments in `pilot-results.csv`. Use anonymous participant IDs and do not put personal information in the repository.

## Analysis and decision rule

Report participant and case counts, completion rate, correctness, unsupported-claim rate, and paired time differences. Report time among correct completions together with all failures; discarding failed or slow attempts can make a weaker system look faster. With such a small sample, treat results as directional and show individual paired outcomes.

Before collecting data, choose whether a 25% reduction in median correct-report time with no observed increase in unsupported claims would justify another pilot. This is a proposed product threshold, not a measured result or statistical guarantee.

An illustrative ROI calculation may later use measured minutes saved × incidents per month × engineer hourly cost. Label each input and keep hypothetical assumptions separate from observed results. Fewer repeated failures and reduced downtime require a longer deployment study.

"""Export local example PosMsr recordings using the reference-validated convention.

No downloads. This checks timestamps, finite angles and joint limits, but does not
claim an independent Jacobian check for each recording (those Jcb files are absent).
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from scipy.io import loadmat


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--raw-root', type=Path, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    out = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / 'public/robot/kuka'
    geometry = json.loads((out / 'kinematics.json').read_text())
    reference = json.loads((out / 'position-validation.json').read_text())
    assert reference['mappingVerified'] and reference['recordingId'] == '05-28-21-25'
    limits = np.array([joint['limitsRadians'] for joint in geometry['joints']])
    for folder, rid in [('collision', '03-15-12-53'), ('contact', '03-22-11-18')]:
        source = args.raw_root / folder / rid
        pfile, tfile = source / 'JK_PosMsr.mat', source / 'JK_MsrExtTrq.mat'
        position, torque = loadmat(pfile)['PosMsr'], loadmat(tfile)['MsrExtTrq']
        assert position.shape == torque.shape and position.shape[0] == 8
        assert np.isfinite(position).all() and np.array_equal(position[0], torque[0])
        assert np.allclose(np.diff(position[0]), .001, atol=1e-9, rtol=0)
        indices = np.arange(10, position.shape[1], 10)
        q = position[1:, 10:].T
        assert np.all((q >= limits[:, 0]) & (q <= limits[:, 1]))
        report = {'mappingVerified': False, 'conventionReference': '05-28-21-25',
            'scope': 'Recorded angles using the convention checked on recording 05-28-21-25; no per-recording Jacobian validation. Body and world frame are schematic.',
            'timestampsExactlyMatchTorque': True, 'allAnglesWithinUrdfLimits': True,
            'referenceValidationSha256': hashlib.sha256((out / 'position-validation.json').read_bytes()).hexdigest()}
        payload = {'recordingId': rid, 'angularUnit': 'radian', 'sampleRateHz': 100,
            'times': np.round(position[0, indices], 3).tolist(),
            'joints': [{'channelId': f'joint_{i+1}', 'values': position[i+1, indices].tolist()} for i in range(7)],
            'validation': report, 'provenance': {'sourceUrl': 'https://zenodo.org/records/21927431',
                'sourcePositionSha256': hashlib.sha256(pfile.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
                'sourceTorqueSha256': hashlib.sha256(tfile.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
                'sourcePath': f'{folder}/{rid}/JK_PosMsr.mat', 'method': 'Every tenth original sample starting at 0.010 s; no interpolation or rounding of angles.'}}
        (out / f'positions-{rid}.json').write_text(json.dumps(payload, separators=(',', ':'), allow_nan=False)+'\n')
        print(rid, len(indices), 'position samples; reference convention, per-record validation not claimed')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

**We’re technically aligned, but your concern about business value is valid.**

**Analyze interval** runs the trained model and calculates measurements. It doesn’t improve the robot or retrain anything. Its potential benefit is faster investigation—but we haven’t measured that benefit yet.

I checked the original challenge brief. :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/sametdegirmenci/Downloads/Aionic_Temporal_AI_Hackathon.pdf" purpose="source"}

| Requirement | Our position |
|---|---|
| Useful problem + open data | Defined; user value unproven |
| TimeNet connector | Built and verified on two recordings; training linkage needs clear proof |
| Trained TSLM + held-out baseline | Present; simple signal features outperform canary-v4 |
| Working demo with evidence | Yes |
| Checkpoint/adapter submission | Handoff still needs completing |
| Agentic sourcing bonus | Scout code merged; demo readiness needs verification |

**The weakness is the current workflow:** we select an already annotated incident and ask the model what happened. That makes its contribution feel small.

I’d prioritize three improvements:

1. **Find incidents worth reviewing across a recording.** Use signal-based candidate detection, then OpenTSLM interpretation—without using publisher markers to find them.
2. **Compare with normal behavior.** Show what changed, which joints differ, and whether similar incidents recur.
3. **Prove time saved.** Give engineers the same investigation task with ordinary charts versus Trace; measure speed and correctness.

A stronger product promise is: **“Turn a long robot recording into a reviewable incident report.”**

I’d build toward that before spending more time on animation. A narrow use case can win; an unproven benefit is the bigger risk.

**Yes—this is the right inspiration.** The useful part is connecting **observations → next action → verification**. Our current UI mostly stops at observations.

For robots, I’d build this workflow:

| Question | What Trace should provide |
|---|---|
| **What changed?** | Find unusual torque events and compare them with normal motion. |
| **What should I investigate?** | Identify responding joints, show similar incidents, and suggest the next evidence to check. |
| **Did the change help?** | Compare recordings before and after an engineer’s adjustment: fewer events, smaller disturbances, faster settling? |

That gives an engineer a practical loop: **find → investigate → change → verify**.

But we cannot honestly copy the slide’s specific maintenance diagnoses or predicted repair outcomes. Our dataset lacks verified faults, repair histories, and outcomes. Canary-v4 also analyzes **1.024-second windows**; it doesn’t currently provide the slide’s long-duration reasoning.

**My recommendation:** make the next feature **“Compare this incident with normal motion”**, followed by a before/after recording comparison. Keep the robot animation as supporting context.

The existing work is a useful foundation. What’s missing is helping the engineer make—and evaluate—a decision.

## My request:
Should I merge these PRs:
 They make Trace credible as a hackathon submission, not just a polished screen.

  - **PR #13 — pilot and checkpoint handoff:** gives the team a real way to test the core business claim:
    whether engineers complete an evidence-backed incident report faster with Trace than with charts
    alone. It also creates the checklist needed to hand over the trained checkpoint safely, with its
    exact identity and missing provenance called out. It does not improve the app itself.

  - **PR #15 — investigation integrity:** prevents a publisher marker click from silently triggering an AI
    answer. The user must select an interval and explicitly run analysis. It also makes exports flag
    missing or mismatched model-input receipts, so an exported investigation can be trusted as evidence
    rather than mixing an answer with the wrong data.

  - **PR #14 — broader real-data access, still unmerged:** lets the backend retrieve exact 1 kHz raw torque
    windows from full authorized recordings on demand. That means Trace can investigate more than the
    small bundled demo excerpts while preserving the model’s strict 7-joint, 1,024-sample input
    contract.

  Together: #13 proves or disproves user value; #15 prevents misleading evidence claims; #14 makes the
  workflow usable on more real recordings.
I’ll check which PRs are already merged and whether #14 is ready.

+# From signal interpretation to a useful investigation
+
+Recommendation, 13 September 2026: keep the KUKA retrospective investigation
+use case for this submission. Expand how much investigation it completes, and
+measure its benefit before expanding into an unrelated prediction task.
+
+The product promise to test is: an engineer can find a recorded incident, inspect
+what changed, compare similar cases and hand off a traceable report with less
+manual work. Reduced downtime and successful repairs are not measured outcomes.
+
+## Highest-value sequence
+
+1. Finish full-recording raw access. PR #14 supplies the opt-in backend adapter;
+   the frontend still needs to request the selected raw window, validate it and
+   update its analysis eligibility. Prove a 7 × 1,024-sample request outside the
+   bundled excerpts. Keep GPU training independent of this integration.
+2. Build a retrospective incident inbox across available runs. Start with publisher
+   markers and clearly labeled deterministic candidate windows, group similar
+   signal patterns, and let the engineer inspect examples. A useful demo question
+   is “Where else did this response occur?” Similarity is not a shared physical cause.
+   Any unannotated-event scan needs false-alarm/missed-event evaluation before claims.
+3. Run the prepared chart-only versus Trace pilot. Measure time to a correct,
+   evidence-backed report and report errors, not just speed. Include model failures
+   and reference-selection mistakes. A small exploratory pilot is useful feedback,
+   not proof of fleet-wide ROI. See PILOT_RUNBOOK.md.
+4. Establish what OpenTSLM adds. The archived signal-feature baseline outperforms
+   OpenTSLM on interaction classification (0.9880 versus 0.8845 macro-F1), and
+   OpenTSLM's usable-summary rate is 77.93%. Improve output reliability on validation,
+   and compare investigation quality/time with and without generated interpretation.
+   Do not tune on the inspected test archive or claim a language-model advantage
+   without evidence. Finish checkpoint provenance and submission handoff.
+
+## How to use the supplied graph inspiration
+
+Use sparse labels linked to precise evidence. The implemented comparison graph
+shows measured selected/reference peaks at original timestamps with leader lines,
+and retains the full seven-joint table behind a disclosure. Preserve separate
+meanings for measurements, publisher annotations and generated predictions.
+
+Do not copy “95% chance of failure in two days” or “no action needed” into this
+dataset's outputs. Canary-v4 interprets 1.024-second contact windows; this does not
+establish degradation, remaining useful life, calibrated probabilities or safe action.
+
+## If a second dataset becomes justified
+
+Choose it only for a concrete task that existing data cannot support, after the
+current pipeline and pilot are complete. A plausible later manufacturing extension
+is tool-wear estimation: the [PHM Society 2010 challenge](https://phmsociety.org/phm_competition/2010-phm-society-conference-data-challenge/)
+provides milling force, vibration and acoustic-emission signals with wear measurements
+after cuts. It offers a measurable maintenance target, but describes CNC cutters,
+not KUKA robot joints. The [NASA repository](https://www.nasa.gov/intelligent-systems-division/discovery-and-systems-health/pcoe/pcoe-data-set-repository/)
+also lists IMS bearing experiments and simulated turbofan degradation.
+
+Either is a separate model/data-contract/evaluation project, not another recording
+for canary-v4. Split by independent tool, bearing or engine histories; evaluate
+forecast error and useful warning lead time. Calibrate any probabilities separately.
+Forecasting can be a roadmap item; a weak last-minute forecast would undermine the
+otherwise reproducible submission. No dataset switch guarantees a judging outcome.

## My request:
Okay, so what is the business value? Like how can we convince them, they might ask why all of this. Like what do we gain? Maybe check what the others are doing too if that's relevant. What do you think?

I’ll pressure-test the value proposition against the challenge brief, our actual evidence, and any public competing projects. Then I’ll give you the strongest honest pitch and the judge questions we need to answer.

The strongest framing is:

> **Trace is Sentry for robot incidents:** after a robot stops, it turns raw telemetry into a traceable investigation package an engineer can review and share.

The value is:

- Less time locating and interpreting incidents.
- Consistent reports across engineers and runs.
- Exact evidence, checkpoint, and input receipt for audits.
- Similar incidents become cohorts for controller improvement and retraining.

A normal AI could interpret a screenshot, but it cannot guarantee exact 1 kHz input, preserve provenance, synchronize replay, separate measurements from predictions, or produce a reproducible report.

The honest weakness: our signal baseline beats OpenTSLM on classification—0.988 versus 0.8845 macro-F1. So we should sell OpenTSLM as the **natural-language investigation interface**, not as the most accurate classifier.

Aionic publicly emphasizes “detect, explain, predict, act.” Their newer TS-Haystack work specifically values finding events inside long signals and explaining the evidence. That strongly supports our next feature: an **incident inbox across recordings with “find similar events.”** [Aionic](https://www.aioniclabs.ai/), [TS-Haystack](https://www.aioniclabs.ai/research/ts-haystack)

Highest leverage now:

1. Run the prepared timed pilot with 3–4 engineers.
2. Add the cross-recording incident inbox and similarity search.
3. Demo a clear before/after: raw charts → defensible report.
4. Avoid unsupported repair or failure predictions.

I couldn’t find public competitor submissions, so guessing their products would be unreliable. Our advantage should be credibility: real data, real trained model, honest baseline, and traceable evidence.

I found no obvious CNN training bug. Validation macro-F1 was 0.990 and test was 0.975, with a normal learning curve and sensible early stopping at epoch 23. Its weak point is onset outliers: median 18 ms, but P90 274 ms.

The OpenTSLM comparison has several real concerns:

The reported checkpoint is explicitly a canary, apparently limited to 8,192 examples and three epochs—not a comparable full-budget run.
It learns indirectly: signal → soft-prompt tokens → language model → generated JSON. Token loss also covers formatting and evidence prose rather than focusing only on classification.
Checkpoint selection uses language-model validation loss, not macro-F1 or parse validity.
22.1% of outputs failed strict parsing.
Evaluation uses summary prompts, while the canary training mixed summary and atomic prompts.
The warm-start path does not explicitly apply the YAML LoRA rank/alpha/dropout settings; it relies on OpenTSLM defaults ([train\_opentslm.py]\(/Users/Student/Downloads/EHL\_Zurich/ysamet/model\_training/src/robot\_observability/train\_opentslm.py:56)).
The comparison branch lacks the OpenTSLM manifest, learning curve, raw predictions, and checkpoint. Its quoted metrics also contain fields not produced by the evaluator committed on this branch, so the result is not fully reproducible.
Conclusion: the CNN run looks valid; OpenTSLM has not yet received a fair, fully traceable training run. I would not conclude that CNN fundamentally beats OpenTSLM until OpenTSLM is retrained at full budget, selected using downstream validation metrics, and evaluated with the same strict typed scorer and record IDs.
